newsitem.title: JAPAN: United says US-Japan air deal likely in two months.
newsitem.headline: United says US-Japan air deal likely in two months.

text.p: An interim aviation deal between the United States and Japan is likely within the next two months, Cyril Murphy, United Airlines' vice president for international affairs, told Reuters on Wednesday.

"(The present talks) should lead to an agreement, and since the two sides have targeted the end of September as a date for achieving an agreement, both the process and the target date, it seems to me, lend themselves to the idea that we are facing the possibility of a successful conclusion in the next two months," Murphy said in a telephone interview.

The two countries completed three days of talks on Wednesday aimed at forging a more liberal aviation accord. The talks included industry and local government officials as well as government officials.
Murphy said a new accord would not just change, but would liberalise the U.S.-Japan aviation market for the first time in the 45 years since the treaty was signed.

"We are very pleased because we think we are on the threshold of an historical event," he said, adding that most of the U.S. airline industry with the exception of Northwest Airlines was behind an interim deal.
The next round of talks are to take place from August 27-29 in Washington, he said.
A shift in Japanese policy towards free market competition was the major reason that had raised chances of a new deal, Murphy said.
But he also said the the issue of whether the ultimate goal of liberalisation should be open skies was still a hurdle in the talks.
He said there were still some people in the United States, worried by past trade relations with Japan, who wanted to hold out for a perfect agreement.
Washington has called on Japan to agree that any interim deal will eventually lead to open skies -- its policy of a free market without government restrictions for international air travel.
Japan has, however, sworn it will never accept open skies, arguing that it will only lead to alliances dominated by U.S. carriers.

Murphy said any liberalisation in the bilateral market would work to the advantage of U.S. carriers which were more cost-competitive, adding that in the long-run Japanese carriers would also benefit as it would force them to lower costs.
He said United was confident it would be able to meet any additional competition from other U.S. airlines that could arise from a new treaty.
Asked about future alliances that could emerge from a new pact, Murphy said United was talking to everybody.

"One of the reasons we are so confident is because we have positioned ourselves well in this coming global marketplace. Once this agreement is in place we are going to hang out a shingle that says open for business."

The choosing of a north Pacific partner would be a key decision that would strategically complete the Star alliance and United would take its time in deciding a new partner, he said. The Star alliance groups Lufthansa, Thai Airways International, SAS, as well as United.
"Rushing in to early marriages has a very high failure rate," said Murphy.
